PhD thesis, Australian National University (open access,http://hdl.handle.net/1885/12885). Front matter, 'Phonology' (following 'Orthography'), p. x; quoting Waterhouse, J. H. L. 1949. catalog_locator: front matter p. x (roman; p. 13), section 'Phonology' (following 'Orthography', pp. ix-x)
catalog_quote: Waterhouse (1949) provided a description of the phonology that is a useful approximation of the full descriptions provided by Tryon (1995) and Davis (2003). Although this was written in reference to Roviana, it is equally applicable to the neighbouring Nduke: The vowels in Roviana have the same sound as in Italian. Of the consonants there is no c, f, w, x or y. ... Z has the sound of z in zenith. In pronunciation, the accent in the great majority of cases falls on the first syllable (1949:6) ... Nduke speakers frequently drop vowels where these fall at the end of a word within a phrase. This can also apply to proper names made up of noun segments, e.g. Kol'bangara instead of Kolobangara (the name of a land estate on the island).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (448 pp., ANU open-access scan, handle 1885/12885) and extracted pp. 12-14 with extracted text. p. 13 (roman p. x) carries the heading "Phonology" right after "Orthography", and the passage is there exactly as quoted: "Waterhouse (1949) provided a description of the phonology that is a useful approximation of the full descriptions provided by Tryon (1995) and Davis (2003). Although this was written in reference to Roviana, it is equally applicable to the neighbouring Nduke: The vowels in Roviana have the same sound as in Italian.. In pronunciation, the accent in the great majority of cases falls on the first syllable (1949:6).. Nduke speakers frequently drop vowels where these fall a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Scales (a long-term Nduke fieldworker) states that Waterhouse's Roviana phonology, including 'the accent in the great majority of cases falls on the first syllable', applies equally to Nduke; i.e. word accent on the first syllable in most words. No Nduke-specific examples are given.
new_statements.exceptions: Only hedged as 'the great majority of cases'; no exceptions listed. Word-final vowels are frequently dropped phrase-internally (Kol'bangara), which is a phrase-level process, not a stress exception.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('in pronunciation'), citation-form style statement transferred from Roviana (Waterhouse 1949:6, dictionary preface). Neighbouring Hoava (Davis 2003:29, first-hand) has first-syllable stress on 2-3 syllable underived words and main stress on the third syllable of 4-syllable words, which is consistent with the transferred rule for short words; whether longer Nduke words behave like Hoava is not stated anywhere.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Nduke (= Duke, nke, duke1237) of southwest Kolombangara, the only surviving variety; the phonology statement is Scales' transfer of Waterhouse's Roviana (rovi1245) description to Nduke, not a Nduke-specific analysis with examples.

sources.citation: Davis, Karen. 2003. A grammar of the Hoava language, Western Solomons. Pacific Linguistics 535. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Mentions Nduke only ethnographically (pp. 15, 20). For Hoava itself (3.4.1, p. 29): two- and three-syllable underived words are stressed on the first syllable; four-syllable words take main stress on the third syllable. Cited by Scales 2003 as one of the two full phonologies Nduke resembles.
